Fotografie de atelier, cu decor pictat și elemente de recuzită: scaune. Prezintă o tânără în port popular se șvabi din Lovin, județul Timiș. Tânăra are în mâna dreaptă o creangă de brad împodobită, recuzită specificii sărbătorii „Kirchweih” (Sărbătorirea hramului bisericii, la șvabii din Banat). Fotografie realizată prin imprimare directă (P.O.P. - printing out process). Pe fotografie, în partea stângă, jos apare ștanțat numele atelierului fotografic și localitatea în care funcționează: „Kossak / Timisoara”. V: Rubricatură de carte poștală. Însemnare manuscrisă, în limba germană, cu stiloul: „Lovriner Tracht” și în limba română: Port de șvabi din Lovrin. Ștamilă parțial descifrabilă: „Deutscher Kulturverein / Temesvár 1926” („Asociația culturală germană / Timișoara). Număr de Inventar MCPR 851.

Portrait of a man (named Ah-fit-che, better known as Pedro Jose Quivera), the governor of San Felipe pueblo, sitting on a blanket, demonstrating the use of a pump-drill, a tool used to drill holes in flat turquoise and shell beads.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), 'the point of the drill is a small flake of flint fastened in a slit in the lower end of the shaft which is tightly wrapped either with a string or sinew.  When the stone point becomes dull it is sharpened by flaking the tip in the same manner that flint arrow points are made.  The wheel is made sometimes of stone, wood, or bone, the former being preferable.  The piece of turquois[e] to be drilled is placed in a suitable cavity in a block of wood and held there by the thumb of the left hand while the drill is manipulated by the right, as shown in the picture.  Turquois[e] and shell bead drilling is extensively practised by the Indians of the Rio Grande valley.'

Two expedition carriers washing in a wide, shallow stretch of the Akobo river near Nyighum village. Evans-Pritchard notes that the expedition made its way down the Akobo towards his base at Pochala during March 1935.

A fenced grave of a commoner situated within a homestead adjacent to a hut. Anuak commoners are buried in a shaft dug in the homestead, with a fence erected around it, the grave itself being kept clean and smoothed with sand.
A woman in Pochala village sweeping clean her compound floor with a stiff grass brush. Behind her is a thatched hut with low eaves and a grass fence.
A homestead with a granary to the left and other huts seen from a distance in open country. Several trees and garden crops can be seen growing around the homestead.

A small domed hut with a low entrance and a short section of fence behind, identified as a dry-season camp (location unknown). For villages situated at the edge of the wet season flood extent such as the districts of Ciro, Oyuaa, and Adongo along the Oboth, and Nyikaani district of the Akobo, it was often necessarily to move in the drought to locations closer to the river for fishing and everyday water needs. Since Evans-Pritchard was in Anuakland during the drought he was able to photograph shelters used during this time of the year.

A man wearing a long textile body cloth, walking through long grass, identified as a nobleman of Digiira village, an area under the influence of the Nyigoc lineage. Evans-Pritchard identifies one of two nobles living in this village, namely Agaanya-war-Uliimi.

A view of grass savannah and scattered trees, characteristic of parts of western Anuakland south of Akobo as far as Utalo on the Oboth and Nyighum on the Akobo. The photo may have been taken during his march back to Akobo in May 1935 along the Oboth river.

Two men hoeing in a seated position with sticks in a field near Pochala village. Predominantly agriculturalists, the Anuak clear the fields (often in forest soil) sometime around March and April and sow in May as the rains come on. Since Evans-Pritchard was in Anuakland during this part of the year only, this indicates that this cleared field is being sown in early May.

Kundi. A small bow harp, with a curved, wooden neck and a resonator made from wood and covered with hide. The resonator is a waisted oval shape, with two points at side and one at each end, and two round holes in the top. There are five plant fibre strings that come out from the resonator and are each wrapped round a cane tuning peg that slots into a hole in the neck. The neck is slightly cracked and two of the strings have broken.

Kundi. A wooden bow harp, with a curved neck that terminates in a detailed carving of a human head with a headdress and a necklace of blue glass beads and fibre. The resonator is pointed at both ends with a scalloped waist, with a slight ridge along the almost-flat top; however, the underside of the resonator has a triangular cross-section. The resonator and part of the neck is covered with hide, and there are two round holes in the hide on the upper side of the resonator. There are five strings, each made from two strands of giraffe tail hair twisted together, that are strung between the resonator and the five tuning pegs that slot though holes in the upper part of the neck. The fourth string is broken.

Kokpo. A basket used for carrying a pot of oil, sometimes used in circumcision ceremonies. A coiled basket with a round mouth, cylindrical body of striped natural and black fibres, and a square base, with four strips of cane attached at each corner to form feet. The rim is reinforced with cane wrapped in black fibre. A conical lid made from thick coiled basketry is attached by fibre, and has a loop at the apex. A long handle of twisted fibre is attached to the rim.

Wili kolungbo. Wooden bowl with two side handles, rounded body, and flat base. A small circular perforation is present in each handle; a piece of raffia is tied to both handles through the perforations. Slits present in wood. Used for food.
Inga ka kpe akoro. Gourd-scraper used in pot-making; roughly circular with one flattened edge.

Ngwa. Walking stick with scorched circular indents along the shaft and a right-angled handle. Extending from the handle is a carved head, featuring scorched detailing, with three vertical scarification marks under each eye.

Ngwa. Walking stick with bands of bevelled carved squares upon the shaft and a right-angled handle. Extending from the handle is a carved head, featuring scorched detailing, with three vertical scarification marks under each eye.
Grass circumcision skirt. Alternating groups of light and dark lengths of grass tied to a cord waistband. Used by boys for dancing. Rolled.

A view of a Zande homestead with a posed group of five women in the foreground showing a variety of Zande domestic objects and activities. These include a trough mortar and pestle, stirring a pot, sorting a pile of eleusine, ?winnowing grain, and grinding flour. Behind the group is a man dressed in a tunic and large pantaloons, holding a very large spear, probably used for hunting elephants or other large animals. Buchta made an excursion to the groups west of the Nile in 1879 setting out from Juba on 7th July and returning there on 26th August.

A full length portrait of a Zande woman in front of a hut carrying a small child in a broad skin carrier on her hip. Buchta made an excursion to the groups west of the Nile in 1879 setting out from Juba on 7th July and returning there on 26th August.
A portrait of two women wearing barkcloth aprons (agbaya), made from the bark of a species of fig-tree (Ficus platyphylla).

Two widows (dekurugbo) in the foreground (with shaven heads, one with string around torso) being ritually anointed with oil at the termination of their mourning period, when a feast is held. After a husband's death widows would have been expected to marry either his brother or another close male relative (levirate).

A group of abinza (witchdoctors) dancing at a gathering held in Evans-Pritchard's own compound on the occasion of the ritual burial initiation of a new member (Evans-Pritchard's servant Kamanga) which facilitated the gathering of data on the abinza corporation. Kamanga's feet can be seen emerging from the hole.
A portrait of a man (identified as Kisanga).

A tuka or spirit shrine in the centre of a homestead, consisting of a split stick, the ends bound at the top, and next to it a taller tree trunk with a gourd (of medicines) hanging from it. Such shrines are sites for medicines or ngua that are invoked to ensure ancestral (spirit) favour for the inhabitants of the homestead. Beyond is a shelter with a roof supported on four columns, possibly with carved capitals, and a chair.

A portrait of a man (identified as Tupoi) with brimmed straw hat (kisikindi), with two other men either side of him, and in the foreground some large wooden vessels. Beyond is a large meeting shelter (possibly type known as baruti). This may indicate that the image was taken at Gangura's court.

A man (identified as Kamanga, one of Evans-Pritchard's servants) posed blowing a magic whistle (kura). Such whistles are mostly worn about the body and are used for a variety of purposes, such as to ward off witchcraft. They are made from plants and horns with magical associations, such as zerengbondo, a type of creeper.

Two boys, one showing a slightly expanded abdomen (associated with malnutrition) and abdominal hernia, standing outside a hut with long eaves almost reaching the ground and a tunnel-like entrance way (probably a sleeping-hut for older children, possibly type known as barumai or dondomo).

Kumbu buda. Pottery container for beer. Globular body with round base. Neck shaped into a human bust; eyes made from small pieces of shell, stone or bone. Both ears are pierced, one with a short length of cane through the piercing; grooved lines below the cheeks indicate scarification. Above the face and below the mouth of the pot is ornamented with semicircular indentations representing hair texture. The upper body is decorated with curving lines of semicircular indentations and small circular impressions.

A three-quarter length portrait of a man (identified as the Gumuz chief) wearing an arabic-style white tunic. Evans-Pritchard notes that he met a small colony of these people, who had come from western Ethiopia in small groups over the years, around Roseires. They were (and are) predominantly muslim and besides agriculture kept small numbers of cattle and other livestock. This seems to have been the first image taken by Evans-Pritchard when preparing for his Dar Fung tour of 1926.

Photograph in a series which records and documents the photographer's brother, carver Hideta Kitazawa, making a Japanese noh mask for the Pitt Rivers Museum [2015.28], commissioned as part of the VERVE Project to be exhibited in a new case display on the subject of 'Woodworking': 'The Wood (Hinoki)/ I use Hinoki wood (Japanese Cypress) for making noh masks. It is found only in one small mountainous, deep valley region in Japan, called Kiso, located near Nagoya. Kiso's harsh climate (with a lot of snow in winter) causes the Japanese Cypress tree to grow very slowly and produces beautiful annual rings. We usually use Hinoki wood that is approximately 200-300 years old and has been stored in suitably dry conditions. This means that the wood is both strong and lightweight./ The timber merchant that I use only supplies Hinoki wood. I have a very good relationship with this timber supplier - and they always supply me with the best quality wood' (caption provided by Hideta Kitazawa).

A group of Mandari women and children resting in the shade of a tree. They are displaying a variety of styles of hair shaving, and a couple are wearing the display beads commonly given by youths to girls that they admire.

A full-length group portrait of three Mandari girls wearing numerous strings of beads around their waists, a youth standing to their left with another youth's arm around him. Girls often wore beads given to them by male admirers, but they did not indicate any age sets or grades amongst the women.

A full length group portrait of some young Mandari girls standing in the shade of a thicket, carrying gourd water containers in net carriers. They have decorated their hair and faces using an ash mixture.
An upper body full face portrait of two Mandari youths in a homestead wearing strings of waist beads, a club tucked under one arm.

An upper body full face portrait of a Mandari youth, wearing a number of strings of rem waist beads. The colour configuration of these beads exhibited relative age-grade status. Age-grades among the western Mandari seem to have been a relatively recent, loosely defined or organized borrowing by youths from their Atuot neighbours, there being no memory of age-grades or even initiation in the past.
Two Mandari women sitting on a low square platform in a homestead, with a girl sitting next to them. The women are wearing bound metal arm and leg ornaments.

A three-quarter length portrait of a Mandari woman leaning against the thatch of a hut, wearing metal arm ornaments and a short fringed apron. She has several bands of vertical cicatrice dots on her abdomen.

A three-quarter length portrait of a man wearing a tunic, holding a small parrying shield and spear (possibly abat, large type used for hunting Buffalo etc.). In the background is a section of garden with manioc growing.

A full length group portrait of two men in uniforms of the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium authority (1899-1955) wearing a belted tunic and a hat with regimental plume, two women in floral European-style dresses standing beside them. Both men have their heads turned half away from the camera, perhaps a military style. Beyond them is a long stone and brick built rectilinear building with a dodgy thatched roof, perhaps a barracks?

A group portrait of three standing men, one in the uniform of the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium authority (1899-1955) wearing a belted tunic and a hat with regimental plume. The other two men wear administration-style shirt and shorts, and may have been employed by the administration locally. Behind them another man stands next to Buxton's vehicle, parked outside a hut.

A portrait of Jean Buxton's Mandari sergeant, Makelele Nyayo, who was charged with looking after her personal safety, sitting cross-legged on the verandah of a colonial brick building next to a girl wearing beaded neck ornaments. Just behind or to the side of the girl another person gestures a hand into the frame above her head.

View of an exterior wall surrounding the Oba's palace in Benin City, with vegetation growing in the foreground, photographed some time in the aftermath of the British military attack on the city.

View of a group of five Edo men, undoubtedly elders or chiefs, being escorted by a uniformed soldier, captioned in black ink below the print 'The first deputation'; they are members of a first deputation (of two) sent by the king (Oba) of Benin to negotiate with leaders of the British military campaign force, sent away shortly thereafter.

View of trees seen in the distance, including one especially tall or prominent tree, apparently on the edge or outskirts of Benin City. A handwritten caption elsewhere describes the place as being '[w]here the attack was made from', i.e. the direction from which the final assault by British troops on the city commenced. The same caption continues: 'The big cotton tree is where the King was to be hanged.'

View of a group of four Edo men, sitting on a bench along the wall of a building, described elsewhere in a handwritten caption as showing 'Captive Bini chiefs'; they are members of a second deputation (of two) sent by the king (Oba) of Benin to negotiate with leaders of the British military campaign force, subsequently held as hostages.

Group portrait of eight men, including British officers and others, standing and sitting – identified as Maj. Frederick Landon (front row, left), Lieut.-Col. Bruce Hamilton (front row, centre), Lieut. John Daniels (front row, right), Capt. Charles Ringer (back row, left), Lieut. O'Shea (back row, second from left), Dr. Felix Roth (back row, centre), Capt. Herbert Walker (back row, second from right) and Capt. Charles Carter (back row, right) – taken inside the king's (Oba's) residence, or palace or 'compound' area, in Benin City, in the aftermath of the British military attack on the city. Clearly visible at the left of the image are a number of commemorative heads and other figures, which were in the process of being collected and removed (elsewhere described in related documentation as 'loot').

A portrait of a woman wearing two elaborate coiled ornaments on her chest, with other neck and ear ornaments. This woman is described in the original documentation as a Terit woman photographed in Luo country, which would probably make her a Tiriki woman. The Tiriki are a sub-tribe of the Luhya of Western Kenya who border the Luo. Her personal adornments, particularly the long beaded earrings and the coiled metal pendants are not particularly Luo. [Gilbert Oteyo 27/04/2005 & CM 25/04/2007]

A Dinka man setting out towards a game path with an animal trap (dang) on his back, consisting of a wooden frame with rope [poor image]. The Powell-Cotton's collected this trap, perhaps from the individual in this image, on the 3rd May 1933, and donated it to the Pitt Rivers Museum. It is likely that this print is a still taken from the cine-film made by Powell-Cotton during this expedition.

A male and female dancer, probably Dinka, in close dancing formation. The man is wearing a feather in his hair, a wide beaded waist band with a small band of probably leopard fur below, a wooden disk arm ornament and is holding a club. The woman, who is stretching her arms back as part of her dance movement, is wearing a long apron, probably goat skin, fringed with beads, as well as cowrie waist bands. Just beyond the pair another pair are dancing together, the male holding his spear aloft. This image resembles several taken of Dinka dances by Godfrey Lienhardt (see for instance 2005.51.427), and may have been given to Evans-Pritchard by him. [CM 17/07/2006]

Young child, standing on a caryatid stool. The caryatid figures represent human beings. The stool is flanked by a long rectangular and richly carved panel on each side, standing upright. The one to the left shows four human figures on top of each other, the on the bottom being a female. The figure on the top represents an European, riding on an animal. He wears a white european dress and a pith-helmet. The panel on the right side shows four human figures as well, the first from the bottom thereby placed above an animal (lizard?). On top of this first figure, showing a male, the carver placed two female figures, the right one being significantly smaller than the left one. On top of them there is again a male figure, above which an animal is shown, similar to the ridden animal on top of the left panel. The carvings and the child are placed in front of a house wall, which is made of bamboo sticks. A vertical rectangular segment of the wall is patterend by a geometric design (see also 1998.11.12).

Full length portrait of Nkanga, the chief of Banju. He is sitting on a traditional stool, which represents an elephant, in front of a house entrance. To his left, a slit-drum stands on the ground. He wears traditional clothing, including a hat, but european shoes. The entrance of the house, which is made of bamboo sticks, is roofed by a canopy, which is made of mats. They show a geometric pattern, due to different coloured fibres.

Three quarter length backside portrait of a nude woman, whose arms, torso and buttocks are with scarifications. She is standing in front of a house wall, holding a pottery above her head. She wears a necklace, made of white beads.

Group of 15 women in front of a house made of bamboo sticks. The door is made of mats, which show a geometric pattern due to different coloured fibres. Three large pillars are supporting the roof. The women are dressed in loincloth, some are decorated with beads. They are wearing necklaces, bracelets, anklets, some are also wearing earrings. The women are holding beaded calabashes in their hands, which are used as palm wine containers for the Fon's exclusive use. The calabashes show different finials as stoppers.

Two men and two boys in front of a house. The chief of Batufam is sitting and covered with a cotton cloth, which only reveals his face. A young boy, also dressed in the same manner, is standing at his left side. Both a flanked by two men, the one to the right wearing only a loincloth, the one to the left is wearing a white shirt and a cap.

Two masks dancers. The mask to the left, called mbap mteng, representing an elephant. Two caryatid stools are on the ground, one with a back showing two large human figures. The stool is shadowed by an umbrella. Both caryatid stools show animals as caryatid-figures. At the left side of the stools stands a male bowl figure, decorated with beads. European-style house, made of bricks. The roof is made of corrugated iron. The upper floor has five windows, which are covered by curtains made of bamboo sticks. These men are building a Luo round house (ot). The construction starts with digging a round trench in which cut poles of different sizes are put and stabilized. Then the horizontal supports of usually young trees or split sisal are tied around them to hold them together as a wall (kor ot). Finally the last wall plate on which the roof (tado) will lie is done and woody vegetation placed in the wall vertically, which is what these men seem to be doing. The entire wall would then be plastered over with earth and cow dung both inside and outside. This plastering process is only done after the roof is put on, lest the rain spoil it. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004 & CM 03/04/2007]

The Rev. J. A. Heasty of the American Presbytarian Mission with his son, who was posted to the newly established Doleib Hill mission station on the Sobat River (roughly six miles from its confluence with the White Nile) in 1925 as a specialist in the teaching of English language. The station was founded in 1902 to provide industrial and agricultural training, a focus encouraged by the British administration. With an increasing demand for English language education from local elites however, the APM responded with another station at Nasir on the Sobat river.

A young girl sits on the ground, weaving a basket. The fronds DIRI are made from the  DURA plant. The basket-maker makes a small square basket base, as in the image. Decoratively carved grave marker by a roadside. SORI and 1945 can be seen carved on the trunk. This is one of a number of old wooden grave markers along the road from Mundri to Amadi.  A village can be seen behind. The road-builders moved the road specially to avoid the grave markers. Informant Andrea told us that these grave markers were used before the current style of  graves as seen in informant Deborah's compound (see 2008.78.1.38). Deborah's account of them was that grave markers were used when there was no body, if the family member had died far away - to bring the 'soul' home. This grave marker has two 'rings' carved at the top. There used to be specialist craftsmen who made the grave markers. Patti Langton [26/05/2009]

A rain-making shrine of an unusual type compared to other Bongo rain-posts (riyak), and rather more like in form a Zande tuka or ancestral shrine. It was situated under a large tree, with ground swept well around it. The female operator of the shrine threw water over it with an invocation to spirits during drought, since she was widely considered to be possessed and closely associated with ancestral spirits. Directly behind it is a grave mound with forked tally grave post.

A stone mound erected over a woman's grave (dodo) with two carved posts tallying the number of large or dangerous animals killed by her husband as a means of honouring her. The post on the right has a tin basin affixed to the top, possibly for receiving offerings.

Two carved wooden funerary figures, one with large horns set on top of a low earth burial mound within a homestead. Not all Bongo graves were marked with a mound of stones, and such mounds were sometimes erected a number of years later at a mortuary ceremony. These carved figures were considered representations of the deceased, put up to honour the individual, but not serving any ritual purpose. Usually accompanied by tallies of animals killed in hunting, the horns on the figure signify the status of the hunter.

Two carvings, one with horn-shaped elongations, tallying the numbers of large animals killed by the person buried beneath, or sometimes the kills of a relative. Graves were commonly grouped together near a settlement (visible in the background). These carvings were understood as a means of honouring the dead but did not have any particular ritual meaning.

A stone mound erected over a man's grave (dodo) surmounted by a short pointed stake with a decorated gourd attached to it. Around the mound are six carved posts tallying different large animals killed by the deceased, one of which (to the right) is also surmounted by a carved likeness of the man. These carved figures were considered representations of the deceased, put up to honour the individual, but not serving any ritual purpose [cloudy image].

A physical anthropology composite image of the profile and full face of a Bongo man, probably photographed during the Seligman's first expedition in 1909-10. This man was probably encountered whilst visiting the Nile region since the Seligman's did not visit Bongo country in Bahr el Ghazal province.

A stone mound near a hut erected over a man's grave (dodo) with three carved posts surmounting the top tallying twenty elephants killed in the hunt by the deceased, placed as a means of honouring him. Around the mound are five more carved posts (some with arrows stuck in them); the first a likeness of the deceased, the next clockwise a forked (horn-shaped) post set up by his son-in-law yet tallying his own buffalo kills. The next (only tip visible) is a likeness of the deceased with a tally of two hippo killed, then a forked post tallying six rhino and lastly a forked post tallying five buffalo.

A wooden carving set next to a grave incorporating a likeness of the deceased wearing a piece of matting as a hat, with notches carved below tallying two hippo killed by the individual. This carving forms a group with five other posts set round a burial mound surmounted by three posts tallying twenty elephants killed.

A figure carving with a small straw hat representing a deceased man, set close to his grave mound also surmounted with hunting tallies, as a means of honouring him. Evans-Pritchard describes this figure as having bead eyes, the face being stained blue with a dye bought from an Arab merchant, and the body being painted red with red ochre.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows the south face of a carved stone stela known by archaeologists as Stela C, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'In size and general appearance this monument closely resembles Stela A. The principal differences are: - That four glyphs form a pedestal to the figures carved on the front and back of the monument instead of a grotesque mask. On the front of the monument (Plate XVI) [ie. this photograph] the two faces in profile near the top are grotesque instead of human faces. At the end of the breastplate are jaguars' heads instead of snakes' heads.' More recent scholarship dates the stela (also known as Monument 3) to 9.17.5.0.0 (Maya calendar), or A.D. 775 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. The monument was created during the later part of the sixty-year reign of K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat and marked the close of an era in the Maya calendar. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place at the height of the city-state's power during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows the west side of a carved stone zoomorph known by archaeologists as Zoomorph B, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'This monument is lying on three large slabs of stone, which are well shown in Plates IX and X. It is carved into the shape of a great dragon, with a human head, bust, and hands issuing from the dragon's mouth. In Plate XII, a, the two great eyes of the dragon, with hanging eyelashes and crossed bands over the eyeballs, can be clearly seen. The upper jaw is raised so that the row of incisor teeth shows above the grotesque mask which surmounts the human head.' More recent scholarship dates the zoomorph (also known as Monument 2) to 9.17.10.0.0, 12 Ahau 8 Pax (Maya calendar), or A.D. 780 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. Identified over the years variously as a tiger, dragon, turtle and toad, the carving is now understood by scholars to represent a supernatural crocodilian, sometimes termed the Cosmic Monster. The monument was created during the later part of the sixty-year reign of K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat and marked the close of an era in the Maya calendar. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place at the height of the city-state's power during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows the south face of a carved stone stela known by archaeologists as Stela D, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'The south face of this monument (Plate XXI) [ie. this photograph] is much damaged. The pedestal is in the form of a large grotesque head. Above this head stands a full-face figure holding in the left hand a tasselled shield with a grotesque full face on it, and grasping in the right hand what I shall term a "manikin sceptre". The stone is so much worn that the hand and sceptre are hardly distinguishable.' More recent scholarship dates the stela (also known as Monument 4) to 9.16.15.0.0, 7 Ahau 18 Pop (Maya calendar), or A.D. 766 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. The monument was created during the later part of the sixty-year reign of K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place at the height of the city-state's power during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

View of a Hopi woman, seated on a rock, combing the hair of a man who is sitting on the ground, with a woman leaning against a wall behind them.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), the 'brush-like comb used combines two articles in one.  A bunch of long round-bladed grass is selected, and around the butt of it, a short distance from the end, a string is tightly wrapped.  The butt-end is utilized as a comb, while the long end is used as a broom, and sometimes as a strainer.  For the latter use, the brush end is flattened by the hand and thumb.  This is held over a bowl, and the goats milk poured through it.  The picture shows some of the details of hair-dressing among the [Hopi].'

View of buildings at Sichomovi pueblo on First Mesa, with a laden donkey (burro) in the foreground.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), Sichomovi '[i]s the middle village on the summit of the same mesa with W[a]lpi and Tewa.  The people of this village belong to the Shoshonan family and are identical in all respects with W[a]lpi.  Their village, however, is less characteristic of the typical terraced formed pueblos, the houses only reaching two stories in height.'

Bottleneck basket with red wool and feather decoration, from unknown collection. Coiled.
Tawahemen. Woven red and white basket with circular rim and square base. Cane around rim, attached with fibre string. Traditional Panare design.

Ewey. Deep basket made of open work cane with a wide mouth, slight shoulder and square base. Ring of cane around the rim, attached to the basket with string, with a small string handle attached to both sides of the basket. Some of the cane has been painted to create a geometric pattern.
Wooden shedstick, beater or weaving sword. Elongated oval with pointed oval cross-section. Decorated with sporadic incised lines which may have resulted from use.

Kamawa', or shoulder bag. The bag is rectangular and made from spotted animal hide, possibly jaguar. A triangular flap at the front of the bag has a knotted string threaded through it. A string shoulder strap is affixed to the top corners using red thread, which has also been used to stitch up the side seams.

Wapa. A shallow, round tray made from plaited basketry with frames of cane attached by fibre to the inside and outside of the rim. Plaited black and natural geometric pattern with a central square with four monkey motifs and a pattern of triangles and lines above and below. Small loop of fibre attached to the frame.
Wapa. A shallow, round tray made from plaited basketry with frames of cane attached by fibre to the inside and outside of the rim. Plaited dark brown and natural geometric pattern.

Areko. Circular headdress. Made of a layered plaited headband, possibly leaf, with a double frame of wood or cane. The feathers are held together with fibre and fit between the two layers. A leaf bundle is present, to be suspended down the back. There are five feathers detached but present.
A chisel formed from the incisor of a capybara, bound with fibre to a long, cylindrical palm wood handle.
Chiquitey; small conical wicker basket with widely separated paired warps. Flat rectangular base and circular opening.

Tamase. Headdress made from two circles of Tamshi bound with black and red cotton; circles are joined on the inner edge. Red and yellow toucan feathers are attached to a woven cotton band which is secured between the two circles.

Patako. Two armbands or arm ornaments, each consisting of a woven red and blue cotton band decorated with striped zig-zagged beadwork. One (.1) features red and white, and green and red beads. The other (.2) features blue and red, and green and red beads. Beads are trade beads. Bands worn by a young girl.
Rattle - On catalogue card: "Rattle of nut shells attached to plaited fibre band. Worn on leg during dances.".

Rice wine container, comprising a tall, handled body and a lid connected to the body by a plant fibre string. The body is made from a cylindrical internode of bamboo, and is divided into sections. The handle is made of hide, with some hair remaining. The lid is of wood, with incised patterns, a spout and a curved handle. The lid does not sit inside the top of the container.
Small basket, with square base and round top. Design in black.
Dish - Wooden dish, with carved illustration and black and white decoration round the brim

Bag - String bag. The actual square bag is made of fibre coloured with five fields consisting of five black stripes each. Attached to the top are 14 loops made of cane which hold the plant fibre string that runs down to the right and left bottom corners of the bag. The string loops on either side and is worn over the shoulders, with the bag worn on the back. When the string is pulled through the cane rings the top of the bag closes.

Platter - Wooden dish/platter carved with human figures, a single face and a deer-like animal with inlaid black and white triangular decoration around the rim. A projection on the rim, probaly used as a handle, forms a carved human figure wearing a hat, shown from the waist. Facing this are two human faces carved in the rim, turned towards each other. two men are carrying the deer.

Tsatsavu. Pair of short, rectangular, women’s leggings. Made of black velvet with green synthetic band stitched along top, which extends to form ties either side. Further panel of black velvet appliquéd to front lower edge, decorated with repeated anthropomorphic faces, wearing ovoid linear headdresses, in orange, green, yellow, white and blue glass beads, intersected by sequins. Row of aluminium discs stitched along top edge of panel; band of beaded diamond motifs along bottom edge of panel.

Valan. Man’s sash of red cotton with central row of white plastic discs, each separated by two flower-shaped sequins. Plaited band of synthetic wool in yellow, green and red strung along centre over white discs. Band of small blue, orange, yellow, green and white beads arranged in triangular or chevron motif along top and bottom of sash, enclosed by aluminium chains, which extend as tassels at one end, and loop at other. Tassel end also decorated with two tassels of coloured beads terminating in metal bells. Reverse lined with blue synthetic fleece and blue cloth, possibly cotton.
Portrait sculpture in plaster of Anhamattu, a Kadar man.

Kirmic. A pair of pink Converse All Star shoes with navy blue polka dots and white laces. The inside of the shoe has a blue and white gingham pattern. The shoes are laced up. There are wear marks on the soles. Each shoe has a white circular converse branded label on the side of the fabric. The shoes are a size 4.
Shallow, round vegetable basket, with flat, bamboo strip as a base
Kareau. Life-sized sculpture in wood. The face is painted with white pigment with nautilus shell eyes and the hair coloured with Reckitt's Blue.
Puchai. A: Container and B: Lid made of Daar wood turned on a hand lathe. Holds millet wine. Used by Yarjung during a ritual. Made by Chunarr (?caste group).

Ten Phahssaa. Bag with shoulder straps made from chemical compost bag. Painted by Yarjung and used as he would use a leather bag Ten Phahssaa. Use as an outer bag for carrying goat skin bundle 1993.36 which contains ritual objects.
Figure, small gilt bronze lion; base of lamp stand. Newar work
Malgai. Blue conical hat with red patterned silk edging and a large tassel at the point of the crown. The ear-flaps are integral and tie under the chin with red ties. Lamb's fur inside.
Shagai Shurgai. Bundle of interlinked metal loops. Each loop is roughly made from a small piece of wire with raw ends. This is part of the knucklebone game (2001.7).

Miniature wooden churn, comprising a cylindrical container (A), a perforated lid (B) and a spatula (C). All parts are made of a pale brown wood, and the container has two silver-coloured metal bands around it.
Costume. Pair of earrings, each having a perforated, jade disc hung on silver ring with sham turquoise setting.

Bracelet, made from a strip of copper alloy, probably brass, which has been bent into a penannular shape. The edge of the bracelet has been decorated with two incised lines and four circular impressions at one end, near to the penannular opening.
Portrait sculpture in plaster of Burunda, a Vedda man

Long length of woven red cotton with striped pattern, decorated possibly a skirt. Stripes of white and black, yellow with lozenge shapes of black, thicker strips of brown with white, and wider strips of red and dark blue. Woven on back-strap loom.
Mixer; Masher - Bamboo mixer used in the manufacture of Tibetan paper. Length of bamboo forms the handle which splits into four, tied together to form a square base with plaited lengths of ?bamboo.
Spinning spool (spindle) and thread, as spun on the thigh. Taken from a deserted Abor house.
Axe or "Dao" with metal blade and vegetable fibre binding on haft.
Rectangular piece of cloth of woven pland 'pud' fibres, made up of two pieces sewn together, natural or light brown in colour.
Oplecko. Woman's shirt. White with embroidered decorations in pink, red, blue, green, and orange around the cuffs, shoulders, and neck. The sleeves end in lace panels. There are ties at the front.

Lajblik. Woman's vest. The outside of the vest is a purple fabric with embroidered flowers and sequin, bead, and ribbon decorations along the seams on both the front and back. A panel of green fabric embroidered with orange, blue, and white flowers is sewn to the bottom and ruffled on the back. Metal fasteners are sewn to the inside at the top and bottom.
White table cloth with lace trimming. The lace trimming has a floral pattern.
Walrus or Narwhal ivory model of a Samoyede family with their sledge and reindeer.

A doll made of turquoise fabric with red, yellow, green, blue, and purple pieces of fabric sewn to the back and the bottom. The head of the doll is made of the top half of a bird's beak with part of the skin of the bird's head attached to the fur. The bird's beak is cracked.
Pin made of blackthorn wood, trimmed and fried in fat, made by Leviathon Pickett. One terminal tapers to a point, the other flat. Pinned onto a letter explaining how the pins are made and used.

Knife with a metal blade and handle possibly made of antler. The handle is in the shape of a boot, with a low heel and decorated with dots and arches. The blade has a straight back, curving towards the points, and a straight blade. Blade is stamped with a makers mark.

Tamata. Votive offering. Stylised representation of a head and neck, hand modelled in yellow/green wax with eyes represented by black-eyed beans. The nose and mouth are stylised and the ears are represented by holes either side of the head. A loop of string protrudes from the top of its head, suggesting a point of suspension.

Tamata. Votive offering of a kidney, hand modelled in green wax. It is an oval object with a shallow groove in the centre of one of the longer sides. There is a loop of string protruding from one of the shorter sides.
Gold plastic disc-shaped protective charm placed on car dashboard. Obverse side has colour print of the Madonna and Child flanked by angels. Simulated wood on reverse.

Tamata. Votive offering. A representation of a child standing in profile with head turned to front, stamped on thin, silver sheet with incised detail. There is a semicircular tab and hole at the top of her head for the attachment of a pin.

Small full-length wooden female figure used for love magic. With a large head and sharply bent elbows and knees. Hands rest either side of back of head and feet at each end of a bar at the base. Tongue visible in oval mouth. Tassels in nose, wrists, waist, neck and one ankle and oval eyes with nassa shell inlay. Very prominent genitals and possible anus at rear.
Lens-shaped wooden head. Raised oval ring and dot eyes, club nose extending in arch to chin. Attached to 1930.277 with native fibre.

Necklace of plaited string work in form of face with 5 short triangular tails giving face star shape outline. Bulbous forehead, cowrie shells for eyes. Ribbed nose-loop with 2 pairs of conus shell hooks bound with string and bast fibre, for nose ornament. Reverse of face has loop in centre and 3 string, feather and red cloth strip tassels attached to loop. Broad neck band ornamented with cowrie and nassa shells at intervals. Some remains of black and red pigment. Neck band fastens by loop on one end and large knot on the other.

A ceramic pot with a wide mouth, upright rim, straight sides and a flat base, with a small handle attached to the rim and a raised ridge just below the rim. Inside covered in a dark red slip, outside a light orange colour with vertical red lines.
A necklace made of spherical brown seeds with vertical ridges. Some of the seeds have small holes on the surface.

Small pot of burnished red ware. Slightly everted rim, short neck and narrow mouth, rounded body and flat base. Decorated above the shoulder and below the neck with linear markings, incised with a fine pointed stick. Parallel lines between which large triangles pointing upwards in which are four rows of stick marks. Black firing marks on side and base.

Globular pot with a flat base, rounded shoulders, narrow neck and everted rim. The interior surface is glazed, with blackened areas extending across the vessel entirety. Below the neck is a band of horizontal notches.

Pot of burnished red ware with everted rim, rounded body and flat base. Decorated below neck with two horizontal bands filled with rows of short diagonal lines. Horizontal band above base. Black firing marks present. Two small chip to the rim.
B: Small, reddish-brown ware beaker. Flat base, black firing marks outside and in.

Spearhead made of Katanga copper. There are two blades, one leaf shaped and one oval, and set across from one another. Both have a midrib, and the shank is twisted below both blades. Split socket with a collar at the opening.
Cane spindle with spherical clay whorl painted with white and orange stripes.
Portrait sculpture in plaster of Lachanttar, a Toda woman.

Male funerary ornament. Band of cotton fabric with white floral designs on maroon background, bordered with blue blanket stitch. From base of band hangs ten large discs from strands of red wool, possibly acrylic, discs with a blue background sewn in blue thread and embellished with beads, probably glass, of silver, green and blue arranged in geometric patterns. Two smaller discs hang from one of the short edges.
A necklace consisting of faceted gold gilt beads strung onto a length of plant fibre.

Bracelet with ovoid pendants, made from brass with possible gilding. Eight pendants with a horizontal ovoid form hanging from a faceted ring; at the centre is one pointed ovoid pendant with incised decoration around the top, hanging from a faceted ring; each pendant alternates with three faceted beads. Strung on white cotton cord.
One of ten paintings of Manipuri tribesmen of Assam, painted by a Manipuri artist. Meiti man. Forms a pair with 1951.764.2.
Headdress  - Palm leaf " crown", worn by young Oraon men as an ornament
Bead necklace. Worn by men and women.
End-blown cane flute with three stops and incised ornamentation.

Choli. Girl's blue bodice with red trim and embroidered decoration. Short bodice, open at the front with ties at the bottom; dark blue cotton with orange to red trim at the end of the sleeves and around the waist, some with woven geometric pattern; embroidered on the front right, right sleeve and back with lines of chain stitch and rows of crosses in yellow and white.

Rotuet ap chok. Iron sword with a leather sheath. The sword has a cylindrical handle with rounded terminal. The sheath has a midrib, with an arched handle on one face. It narrows at the terminal and is bound in a coil of metal.

Simple or self bow with sinew string. Wooden bow with circular cross-section tapered at either end; coil of copper wire around one end; wrapped with plant fibre at one end to prevent string slipping; remains of string attached at one end.

Korket. A hearth. Carved wooden stick of sub-cylindrical shape with ends that taper to a point. One end has two holes that show evidence of fire damage; caused by the friction of a drill. Poinik (fire-stick) consists of a korket (hearth) used with a kirkit (drill) to start a fire by hand through surface friction.

Model house on wooden stilts. Split level house with pitched roof and small extended porch; two ladders leading up to openable doors made from slats of wood tied together with nylon cord; walls, roof and two openable window made from leaves stitched together with pink plastic ribbon; openings decorated with knotted pink and natural plant fibre and with pieces of cotton cloth; ties of plastic ribbon, nylon cord cotton cord and plant fibre used throughout; two rectangular woven mats inside the house.
Square-ended sword with iron blade and wood handle. Also wood scabbard or sheath, open on one side, and a belt of plaited thread

A wooden box (.2) containing five cigarettes (.3-7). The box is rectangular, with a hinged lid that is decorated with an incised image of St George slaying a dragon. The picture is coloured with black, red, and green pigment. The sides of the box feature a band of decoration, and the bottom is decorated with a picture of a priest. There are five cigarettes in the box, along with a small amount of loose tobacco that has fallen out of the cigarettes.
A man’s brown leather belt with a rectangular metal buckle and a small purse attached at the buckle end. The purse is fastened with a metal stud.
Katshula; Kaliposhe. Red fez hat with black tassel. For festive wear.
Lapudzi. Pair of woollen socks knitted with a ribbed cuff in stripes of navy, blue, purple, orange, maroon and green. Heels reinforced with a piece of woven brown material. Tied together.
A rectangular black silk sash made from two panels stitched together in the middle, with a blue trefoil brocade design across the fabric. Hemmed along three edges.

Beaded necklace, comprising a tubular loop decorated with coloured glass beads, with a hanging triangular ornament at the bottom. The tube has diagonal stripes in blue-green, yellow, blue, and green, with a multicoloured section on one side. Loops of blue, green, black, yellow, and red are attached at intervals around the tube. The hanging ornament has a triangular pattern in yellow, blue, green, and black, with hanging loops of green.

A small wooden stool or possibly a headrest. Consisting of an upside down hemisphere with a cylindrical shaft and then a smaller hemispherical base. Carved in relief from a single piece of wood. Tied around the central shaft is a loop of twisted plant fibre string. There are chips missing from the base.
Long necklace made of chips of ostrich shells. Shells have been shaped into rough circles and threaded onto fibre cord.
Feather ornament. Tip of two ostrich feathers layered together, the back feather is pink, dyed from local clay. The front feather is black. Bound together as the stems with plant fibre.
Bleeding arrow with a wooden shaft and metal head. The head is rounded and attached to the shaft possibly with hide. The fletchings have come away and are missing.

Small, finely-woven basket (.1) with a lid (.2). The basket is cylindrical, although the sides round inwards towards the base, and the lid is conical. The basket has been woven with a green triangle pattern, and the top of the lid in also green.

Royal oval wooden meat-dish of musogo wood, possibly used by King of Bunyoro, Andereya Bisereko Duhaga II. Body tapered and stained red with grooved scorched festoons along the rim. With 12 broadly triangular legs upon a concave oval base.
Enkate. Rest for milk pot. A high ring stand made of plaited black and brown bark. Foundation probably of wood.
Oval food bowl or beer cup with a pedestal foot and tapering body. Along the rim are grooved festoons. Evidence of historic damage and partial reconstruction; part of rim is missing.

Rattle. Four wooden sticks, each stick has four hollow seed pods containing seeds. They are held together with twine at one end and cloth at the other end. One stick contains just three seed pods, another pod is damaged.

Nyege. Rattle made from a gourd, the globular part of the gourd is filled with seeds and has small circular holes pierced across the surface. A hole at the top is filled with a cotton fibre stopper. The handle is made from the stem of the gourd and has a loop of fibre threaded through a hole at the end.

Royal drum, with a rounded wooden body and a truncated conical base. The lower part of the body is covered with a casing of ox hide, and the head is covered with an ox hide skin. The two pieces of hide are held in place with straight lacing, made from thin twisted strips of leather. The body is decorated with strings of plaited fibre, strings of cowrie shells, small pink beads a couple of,large blue beads, black seeds and a horn from a ram.
